How I Did It: Barrel Jump

by Sal, Galaxy Zone Arcade

Sal remembers the original cabinet

1981, and suddenly every kid in Portland had barrel-jumping calluses on their thumbs. I had the real machine wedged between two pinball tables up front, and I swear the girder-climbing one got more foot traffic than the popcorn machine. There was a kid, must've been ten, who came in every day after school with exactly one quarter and could clear three barrels in a single jump. Never made it to the top. Never once complained either. Just fed the machine his quarter and tried again.

What the remodel changed

The old version I coded myself last year had barrels that would just teleport past you if the frame rate hiccuped — same deltaTime trick as always, now everything from your walk speed to the barrel roll is tied to actual seconds instead of "however many ticks happened to run." The big thing the crew added this time is the ladders — some of them don't even connect all the way through anymore, which sounds like a bug but it's on purpose, it's a trap, and it makes you sweat a little climbing up not knowing if you'll dead-end. And that hammer power-up now really commits you — you can't jump or grab a ladder while you're swinging it, which is exactly the kind of tradeoff that used to make me yell at the cabinet in '82.

The spell that did it

Build our Donkey Kong game against the shared engine. Six sloped girders connected by ladders — make a couple of the ladders broken, dead ends that don't fully connect. Barrels roll down from the ape and sometimes take a ladder toward the player instead of just rolling off the end. Jumping clean over a barrel should feel great — sound, floating score text, bonus for clearing more than one in a jump. Two hammer pickups that make you invincible for a few seconds but you can't jump or climb while you're swinging it. A fireball that wanders the stage and only the hammer can stop. Bonus timer ticking down, reach the captive before it hits zero.

Under the hood

  • Every girder is just two height values — one for the left edge, one for the right — so walking across it and sliding down the slope is one line of math, no separate "ramp" logic bolted on.
  • Jumping over a barrel is detected by watching which side of you the barrel is on before and after each tick — the instant it flips from one side to the other without you two touching, that's a clean clear.
  • The fireball doesn't just wander — it re-checks which ladder gets it closer to whatever row you're standing on every second or so, same as I imagine the real cabinet's chip must have done it, just with fewer transistors.
  • Falling more than one girder height in a single jump is what kills you — land on the very next girder down and you're fine, miss it and it's a long way down.
